analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run national health insurance program covering doctor, hospital, dental, and nursing care, funded by a new 5% value-added tax.
analysis.headline: Dingell's national health insurance bill, introduced in January 2009 with no cosponsors, was referred to two House committees and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have created a national health insurance program run through the Department of Health and Human Services, covering doctor visits, dental care, hospital stays, home nursing, and extras like eyeglasses, for anyone who had worked a minimum amount or was on Social Security, plus their dependents. Patients could choose any doctor or hospital that signed up. It would have been paid for by a new 5% value-added tax on most sales and services, with the money going into a National Health Care Trust Fund. The bill was referred to two House committees and died there without a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Every eligible person—broadly, anyone with a minimal recent work history or receiving Social Security, plus their dependents—would gain guaranteed coverage for doctor, dental, hospital, nursing, and auxiliary services with free choice of provider and no premiums or deductibles for covered care. Medicare beneficiaries would gain coverage of services Medicare does not pay for, including deductibles and coinsurance. People in underserved areas would gain from provisions aimed at expanding health personnel and facilities, funded by training grants.

how_it_helps.text: Made doctor, dental, hospital, home-nursing, and auxiliary services (including eyeglasses and expensive drugs) available as a right to every eligible person, with free choice of physician and no premiums or deductibles for covered care.
Prohibited discrimination by race, creed, or color in providing services and in allowing providers to participate, and let patients choose any qualified practitioner nationwide.

Directed federal allotments toward states and local areas where health personnel and facilities were below standard, aiming to fix shortages in rural and underserved areas, with grants for training health professionals.
Gave Medicare beneficiaries coverage of the services Medicare does not pay for, including deductibles and coinsurance, and required a study of eventually folding Medicare into the new program.

analysis.who_pays: Nearly everyone buying goods and services would pay through the new 5% value-added tax on commercial transactions, with exemptions for food, housing, medical care, exports, and government and nonprofit entities. Employers and businesses would collect and remit the tax. Private health insurers would lose most of their market for basic coverage, since the national program would pay for care the way Medicare does.
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers, via a new 5% sales tax

drawbacks.text: The bill was financed by a new 5% value-added tax on nearly all commercial sales and services—a broad consumption tax that, because lower-income households spend more of their income, falls comparatively harder on them than an income tax would.

Eligibility was tied to having worked and earned a minimum amount in recent quarters, so people with little recent work history were covered only if a public agency agreed to reimburse the fund for their care—gaps that could leave the poorest Americans in a separate, lesser channel.

Benefits were limited: hospital stays were capped at 60 days per year (with mental-health hospitalization excluded after 30 days), and dental, home-nursing, and auxiliary services could be limited if the Board found personnel, facilities, or funds inadequate.

The bill layered a new national program alongside Medicare, giving Medicare beneficiaries only gap-filling coverage while directing a study of eventually folding Medicare in—leaving two systems to run during any transition.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit—universal coverage for doctor visits, hospital care, dental, nursing, and eyeglasses with free choice of provider—would have been large for ordinary people, and funding it through a broad 5% value-added tax spread the cost across all consumption rather than onto the sick. The drawbacks are real: a new national payroll-linked tax is a heavy lift in any economy, the eligibility rules keyed to work history would have left some jobless people dependent on state reimbursement payments rather than automatic coverage, hospital stays were capped at 60 days a year, and dental, home-nursing, and auxiliary services could be scaled back if money or personnel ran short. The administration—local boards, state plans, a federal fallback—was also complex and untested. But the core design was coherent, and the bill never received even a committee hearing where its costs and benefits could be argued.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on the first day of the 111th Congress, sent to two House committees, forwarded to a health subcommittee, and never heard from again; no other member signed on and no vote was ever taken.

narrative.text: John Dingell introduced the National Health Insurance Act on January 6, 2009, the opening day of the 111th Congress.
Not a single one of the 435 House members signed on as a cosponsor.

The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees, and on January 14, 2009 to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Health; the record shows no hearing, no markup, and no further action.
The 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and the bill died in committee without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The private health insurance industry kept its role as the payer for employer-based coverage, since the bill that would have replaced it never advanced; members of Congress avoided a vote on a new national tax.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private insurers and the status quo

for.name: Rep. John D. Dingell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the 111th Congress; it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and never held a hearing or markup on it; it was sent to a Ways and Means health subcommittee and remained there.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so no partisan split is recorded; the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party, and Congress instead debated a different health overhaul (the Affordable Care Act) in 2009-2010.

industries.note: A national health insurance program paying providers directly would displace most private health coverage, removing the industry's core role as the middleman for working-age health care. The bill did allow voluntary health plans to help deliver services, but not to sell the basic coverage.

They would gain a guaranteed payer for patients who today go uninsured, but would give up billing flexibility and face government-set reasonable-cost payment rates for hospital care. Many would trade autonomy for stable revenue.

Not an industry, but the bill's direct beneficiaries: tens of millions of people who today face unpredictable medical bills would have had doctor, hospital, dental, and nursing care covered as a right.
